battle.title: Scale It Up or Out
battle.description: Bigger box or more boxes? Pick wisely when the traffic roars.

options: Adding more identical machines behind a load balancer
Copying the database to another region
Splitting one service into smaller services
Adding more CPU or RAM to an existing machine
questions.answer: Adding more CPU or RAM to an existing machine
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling (scale up) makes one machine bigger. Adding machines is horizontal scaling (scale out); replication and microservices are different strategies.

questions.text: What is a key limit of vertical scaling?
options: It always requires rewriting the application
One machine has a hardware ceiling and remains a single point of failure
It only works for stateless services
questions.answer: One machine has a hardware ceiling and remains a single point of failure
questions.explanation: Even the biggest server has a maximum size, and if it fails everything fails. The upside is simplicity: usually no application changes are needed.

questions.text: A news site's traffic spikes 20 times on election night, then falls back. Which approach fits best?
options: Buy one huge server and keep it running all year
Upgrade the RAM on the current server that night
Autoscale stateless web servers behind a load balancer
Show users an error page once capacity is exceeded
questions.answer: Autoscale stateless web servers behind a load balancer
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling with autoscaling adds servers for the spike and removes them afterwards, so you pay only for what you use. A single huge server is costly and still has a ceiling; a RAM upgrade means downtime.

questions.text: A small internal app has one relational database that is running out of CPU, and the team is two people. What is the sensible first step?
options: Move it to a larger instance (scale vertically)
Rewrite the app into microservices first
Replace the database with a different data model
questions.answer: Move it to a larger instance (scale vertically)
questions.explanation: Scaling up needs no application change and is quick. Sharding adds major complexity, so it is saved for when the biggest practical machine is no longer enough.

questions.text: Five servers handle 200 requests per second each, and the load is 900. What does the program print for utilisation percent before and after one server fails?
questions.explanation: Before: 900 / (5 x 200) = 90%. After one failure: 900 / (4 x 200) = 112%, so the survivors are overloaded. Horizontal scaling needs headroom (N+1 capacity) to survive failures.
